statements.quote:
This paper aims to provide an initial answer to these questions 
through a preregistered, two-­phase experimental online study on 
written creative output (see Fig. 1 for the experimental design and 
Materials and Methods for details) (16).
statements.locator: p. 1, Introduction, final paragraph

statements.quote:
Par-
ticipants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: Human-­
only, Human with one GenAI idea condition, and Human with five 
GenAI ideas (see table S1 for balance across conditions).
statements.locator: p. 2, Introduction, first paragraph

statements.quote:
After completing their story, 
writers were asked to self-­evaluate their story on novelty, usefulness, 
and several emotional characteristics (see section S1 for all study 
questions).
statements.locator: p. 2, Introduction, second paragraph

statements.quote:
In the second phase, the stories composed by the writers were 
evaluated by a separate group of N = 600 participants (“evaluators”) 
(see table S2 for balance across conditions).
statements.locator: p. 2, Introduction, third paragraph

statements.quote:
All stories were evaluated by multiple evaluators on novelty, 
usefulness, and several emotional characteristics, which comprise 
key outcome variables related to our main research question (see 
section S1).
statements.locator: p. 2, Introduction, third paragraph

statements.quote:
The results of these ex-
ploratory analyses are included in section S5.
statements.locator: p. 2, Introduction, final paragraph

statements.quote:
As part of our preregistration, we tested whether the baseline Human-­
only condition differed from the combined generative AI conditions. 
We find that generative AI assistance increases both the novelty and 
usefulness of stories (results are discussed in section S4). To better 
understand how greater availability of generative AI ideas affects the 
enhancement in creativity, we follow our preregistration to estimate 
the causal impact of the two generative AI conditions separately.
statements.locator: p. 2, Results, Baseline versus generative AI conditions, first paragraph

statements.quote:
We find that, while having access to one generative AI idea leads to 
somewhat greater creativity, the most gains (and statistically signifi-
cant differences in our preregistered indices) come from writers who 
have access to five generative AI ideas (Fig. 2A; fig. S1 shows a violin 
plot of raw data).
statements.locator: p. 2, Results, Baseline versus generative AI conditions, third paragraph

statements.quote:
With respect to novelty, writers in the Human with one GenAI idea condition experience an increase of 5.4% (b = 0.207, 
P = 0.021, see table S3) over writers without generative AI access, 
whereas writers in the Human with five GenAI ideas condition show 
an increase in novelty of 8.1% (b = 0.311, P < 0.001) over writers 
without generative AI access.
statements.locator: pp. 2-3, Results, Baseline versus generative AI conditions; sentence spans the page break and cites table S3

statements.quote:
The novelty and 
usefulness index results are qualitatively unchanged when we in-
clude evaluator fixed effects, story order fixed effects, story topic 
fixed effects, and an indicator variable that equals one if the writer 
accessed at least one generative AI idea (see table S4).
statements.locator: p. 3, Results, Baseline versus generative AI conditions

statements.quote:
In contrast, writers self-­assessing their own stories show no sta-
tistically significant differences in the novelty and usefulness be-
tween authors who were offered generative AI ideas and those who 
were not (see table S5).
statements.locator: p. 3, Results, Baseline versus generative AI conditions

statements.quote:
As illustrated in Fig. 2B, we find that stories written by writers with 
access to generative AI ideas are more enjoyable (Human with one 
GenAI idea condition: b = 0.216, P = 0.028; Human with five GenAI 
ideas condition: b = 0.375, P < 0.001, see table S6) and are more likely 
to have plot twists (Human with one GenAI idea condition: b = 0.384, 
P < 0.001; Human with five GenAI ideas condition: b = 0.468, 
P < 0.001).
statements.locator: p. 3, Results, Exploratory analyses: Emotional characteristics, second paragraph

statements.quote:
Again, writers’ self-­assessments of their own stories show no sta-
tistically significant differences in the story characteristics across 
conditions (see table S7).
statements.locator: p. 3, Results, Exploratory analyses: Emotional characteristics, final paragraph

statements.quote:
First, we look at whether different writers engaged with genera-
tive AI more than others: We do not find differences between more 
creative writers and less creative writers in how frequently they ac-
cessed generative AI ideas in the two generative AI conditions (see 
table S8).
statements.locator: p. 4, Results, Heterogeneity by inherent creativity, first paragraph

statements.quote:
Next, we interact the continuous DAT score with our conditions 
(see tables S9 and S10 for results on all outcome variables).
statements.locator: p. 4, Results, Heterogeneity by inherent creativity, second paragraph

statements.quote:
Figure 3 
presents graphs that show the differential effect of generative AI ideas 
on select variables, based on the inherent creativity of the writer (see 
fig. S2 for graphs of the remaining outcome variables).
statements.locator: p. 4, Results, Heterogeneity by inherent creativity, second paragraph

statements.quote:
Our results show that hav-
ing access to generative AI ideas makes a story more similar to the 
average of other stories within the same condition (Human with one 
GenAI idea condition: b = 0.871, P < 0.001; Human with five GenAI 
ideas condition: b = 0.718, P = 0.003, see table S11).
statements.locator: p. 4, Results, Similarity of stories, second paragraph

statements.quote:
We collected a range of additional (exploratory) out-
comes that are not directly related to our primary (preregistered) 
research questions and therefore not included in the main text, but 
which we briefly discuss here to inspire future directions of research 
(see section S5 for details).
statements.locator: p. 6, Discussion, paragraph beginning Third

statements.quote:
Three participants in the Human-­only condition admitted to using 
generative AI during their story writing exercise and—as per our 
preregistration—were therefore dropped from the analysis, result-
ing in a total number of writers and stories of 293.
statements.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, Writer study and experimental conditions, first paragraph

statements.quote:
(As described above, if 
writers in the Human-­only condition answer “yes” to this question, 
they were not included in our main analysis, as per our preregistra-
tion. In section S3, we present evidence that suggests that the writers 
in the Human-­only condition likely did not use generative AI outside 
of the experimental interface.)
statements.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, Writer study and experimental conditions, fourth paragraph

statements.quote:
Section S6 provides an illustrative overview of the kinds of stories 
produced by the writers in the three conditions: To provide breadth, 
we include stories that score at the top, median, and lower ends of the 
distribution for the novelty and usefulness indices in each condition.
statements.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, Writer study and experimental conditions, final paragraph

statements.quote:
Section S7 shows screenshots of the interface presented to writer par-
ticipants in each of the three conditions.
statements.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, Writer study and experimental conditions, final paragraph

statements.quote:
Screenshots of the interface presented to evalua-
tor participants are shown in section S8.
statements.locator: p. 8, Materials and Methods, Evaluator study, continuation of first paragraph

statements.quote:
For our preregistered indices, we followed Harvey and Berry’s defi-
nition of creativity in terms of novelty and usefulness (12), which 
draws on a diverse range of interpretations of creativity in the litera-
ture. Unless otherwise noted, all outcome (dependent) variables 
were assessed on a nine-­point scale from 1 (not at all) to 9 (extreme-
ly) to capture disagreement versus agreement with a statement or a 
question. The exact wording for each statement or question is shown 
in sections S7 and S8.
statements.locator: p. 8, Materials and Methods, Outcome variables, opening paragraph

statements.quote:
The study was preregistered at AsPredicted.org (ID 136723); a copy 
of the preregistration is included in section S9.
statements.locator: p. 8, Materials and Methods, Preregistration and ethics approval

statements.quote:
This PDF file includes:
Sections S1 to S9
Tables S1 to S18
Figs. S1 to S6
statements.locator: p. 8, Supplementary Materials

statements.quote:
We are grateful to S. Vincent for excellent research assistance and 
programming support.
statements.locator: p. 9, Acknowledgments, first sentence

statements.quote: Data curation: A.R.D. and O.P.H.
statements.locator: p. 9, Author contributions

statements.quote:
Data and materials availability: All data and code needed 
to replicate these analyses are available at Dryad: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.qfttdz0pm. All 
other data needed to evaluate the conclusions in the paper are present in the paper and/or 
the Supplementary Materials.
statements.locator: p. 9, Data and materials availability

Original embedding vectors are not included, but texts, stored similarity outcomes and code naming text-embedding-ada-002 are available. Computing summaries of the deposited similarity scores needs no API key; recomputing embedding-based diversity requires an embedding implementation. No analysis scripts, external model APIs or package-install commands were run.

what_we_could_compute: final.open_items[0]: Recover the Human-only analyzed count directly (95) and analyzed counts for all three arms (95/100/98), rather than infer the control count by subtracting paper totals.

final.open_items[2] and [3]: Join evaluators_stories.dta to creators.dta by story_id, retaining the 3,519 matched ratings, and average each outcome within writer_id. For S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O4 through S1-O9, and S1-O12 through S1-O17, compute per-writer means, arm means, between-writer SDs, SEs and outcome-specific analyzed counts. Keep eval_id for reanalysis of evaluator dependence or reproduction of the paper's evaluator-clustered models. Writer self-ratings for S1-O11 are already one row per writer. The linked data also permit the separate and pooled-AI contrasts.

final.open_items[2]: Compute arm means, SDs and SEs of the deposited sim_cstories outcome (S1-O3) and sim_idea anchoring outcome. All 293 stories are linked to writer and arm, so alternative text-based diversity measures and a correctly specified leave-one-out measure can be computed from the texts. Original embedding vectors are absent; exact embedding regeneration and the code/paper discrepancy about including the focal story require attention.

final.open_items[1]: Recover recorded allocation and exclusion counts from the raw writer file: 309 consenting rows have a condition (100 human, 103 human_1AI, 106 human_5AI), including all 13 non-completers (2/3/8). Some condition labels exist for participants stopped at Overview or TenWords; these counts do not independently establish when the assignment was implemented or displayed.
final.open_items[8]: Inspect the deposited comparison-idea text and processing code to resolve the topic-versus-condition pool description; the Stata sampling code filters on writer_topic.

final.open_items[9]: Reproduce novelty/usefulness contrasts and their uncertainty from the linked ratings to assess the one-idea significance statements. No new outcome estimates were calculated or inserted into the screening form.

notes: Checked 2026-10-09. Read the entire 56,937-character, 362-line markdown conversion in three consecutive chunks, including references, acknowledgments and the final publisher information page. The source PDF has the 9-page article plus a tenth information page; the listed Supplementary Materials (sections S1-S9, tables S1-S18, figs. S1-S6) are not actually included. All statement quotes were checked against PDF text with PyMuPDF and retain extracted line breaks, discretionary hyphens and nonbreaking spaces; the one sentence crossing pp. 2-3 was joined across the page boundary without the intervening caption. No additional availability statements occur in the final information page. Public participant-level data, assigned arms, evaluator and self-rated outcomes, and texts for all 293 analyzed stories were confirmed by reading both processed data files, reading both raw CSVs, and verifying the story_id join.
